chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
s
Satélite
Torneio que premia tickets para outro torneio de
buy-in maior.
SB
Sigla em inglês para “small blind” ou “pequeno cego”.
Posição à esquerda do botão e antes do big blind.
Recebe esse nome por ser obrigado a apostar
metade do valor do blind.
Scary card
Termo em inglês para “carta assustadora”. Carta que
trava a ação dos jogadores, geralmente cartas altas
que completam alguma pedida.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Exemplo: flop Q-J-9. No turn, scary cards
poderiam ser: K ou J que formariam um straight
draw.
SCOOP
Sigla de Spring Championship of Online Poker. Série
anual de torneios de poker online, realizada no
Pokerstars desde 2009.
Seat charge
Termo em inglês para “taxa de assento”. Valor
cobrado para entrar em uma mesa de cash game.
Second Barrel
Termo em inglês para “segundo barril”. Apostar no
turn depois de apostar no flop.
Second nuts
Termo em inglês para “segundo nuts”. É uma gíria
estrangeira para a segunda melhor mão que pode
ser formada de acordo com as cartas no board.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Exemplo: Você segura Q8o e bate o flop J-T-9
com naipes diferentes. A sua mão (QJT98) só
perde para  um KQ (KQJT9) que seria o nuts.
Curiosidade: 22ehnutzz ganhou o 21º bracelete do
Brasil. Quase ele foi o 22º! 
Semi-blefe
Aposta que não tem um valor pronto mas pode
melhorar e formar uma mão forte.
Séries
Maratona de torneios online.
Sessão
Período de tempo que o jogador se mantém em jogo
contínuo.
Set
Trinca feita com um par pronto na mão e outra carta
no board.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Set value
Termo em inglês para “valor de trinca”. Preço
favorável a pagar para ver o flop com o objetivo de
acertar uma trinca quando se segura um par.
Exemplo: “no começo de torneio eu gosto de
pagar para ver o flop com todos os pares porque
tenho muito set value nessa fase”.
Sharkscope
Site que coleta estatísticas e resultados de
jogadores em torneios de poker online.
Exemplo: “para ter seu gráfico no sharkscope, é
preciso habilitar seu nick em cada site”.
Shootout
Palavra em inglês para “tiroteio”. Modalidade de
torneio onde as mesas são jogadas até que reste
apenas um jogador para que então novas mesas
sejam remanejadas com os vencedores de cada
mesa.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Short handed
Termo em inglês para “de mão curta”. Refere-se à
mesa com um número menor de jogadores em
relação à sua capacidade máxima. Em mesas de até
nove jogadores, o short handed pode ser
considerado quando há menos de cinco jogadores.
Short stack
Termo em inglês para “pilha curta”. Refere-se a uma
pilha pequena em quantidade de fichas ou big blinds.
Geralmente, é considerado abaixo de 15 big blinds.
Shove
Palavra em Inglês para “empurrão”. Ato de empurrar
todas as fichas para o centro da mesa.
Sinônimos: All-in ou Push.
Showdown
Palavra em inglês para “confronto”. Ato de mostrar
suas cartas para verificar quem tem a melhor
combinação de mãos. Pode ocorrer em qualquer
rodada de apostas desde que dois jogadores se

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
envolvam em um all-in.
Showdown value ou Valor de Showdown
Quando uma mão não acertou nada no board, mas
tem chances de superar a mão do oponente no
showdown. Exemplo: mãos com A-high.
Simple 3-Way
Software de estudo que analisa situações pré-flop e
pós flop em cenários com 3 jogadores envolvidos.
Sit and Go
Termo em inglês para “sentar e ir”. São torneios com
capacidade máxima de jogadores que inicia assim
que as vagas forem preenchidas.
Size
Palavra em inglês para “tamanho”. Refere-se à
tamanhos de apostas.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Slow play
Termo em inglês para “jogo lento”. Jogar uma mão
forte de forma passiva na intenção de esconder a
força da mão para enganar o adversário; apenas
pagar quando tem uma mão forte para aumentar.
Exemplo: “aquele jogador sempre faz slowplay
com flushes. Finge que é uma decisão difícil
para enganar os outros caras”.
Slowroll
Palavra em inglês para “desaceleração”. Demorar
para agir com uma mão forte, de forma a
demonstrar uma decisão difícil quando não é.
Exemplo: “aquele jogador sempre faz slowroll
com AA. Finge que é uma decisão difícil para
irritar o adversário”.
Snap
Palavra em inglês para “estalo”. Indica uma jogada
muito rápida.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Exemplo: “Eu fui de snap all-in no river, fiquei
assustado quando o vilão deu snap call. Você
tinha que ver, ele snap pagou muito confiante.
Mas minha mão era muito boa e puxei o pote”.
SNG Coach
Ferramenta do ICMizer em que se pode treinar
cenários de all in pré-flop sem precisar investir
dinheiro.
Solver
Palavra em inglês para “solucionador”.  São
chamados os softwares de estudo que solucionam
jogadas em diferentes cenários.
Spades ou “espadas”
Naipe do baralho, indicado pelo símbolo
Spew
Palavra em inglês para “vomitar”. Termo usado para
se referir a um perfil de jogo excessivamente

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
agressivo nas retas finais, com grandes chances de
queda.
Split Pote
Termo em inglês para “pote dividido”. Quando os
jogadores possuem a mesma mão no showdown, o
pote é dividido entre eles.
Exemplo: você segura AJ e seu oponente AT no
board A-K-Q-5-Q. Vocês chegam no showdown
com a mesma mão: A-A-Q-Q-K e dividem o
pote.
Spot
Palavra em inglês para “o ponto”. Indica qualquer
situação observada, vivenciada ou imaginada.
Exemplo: “tenho dificuldades em jogar spots de
3bet fora de posição”.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
SPR
Sigla em inglês para Stack to Pot Ratio ou “proporção
entre stack e pote”. Divisão entre o valor do stack
efetivo e o tamanho do pote. 
Quanto maior o SPR, mais possibilidades de jogadas
você tem no pós-flop.
Squeeze
Palavra em inglês para “espremer”. É um 3bet pré-
flop contra dois ou mais jogadores envolvidos na
mão. Quando alguém abre open raise e qualquer
jogador dá call, o seu 3Bet se chamará Squeeze.
SRP
Sigla para Single Raised Pot ou “pote de único
aumento”. Mão onde ocorreu apenas um raise pré-
flop.
Stack
Palavra em inglês para  “pilha”. Pilha de fichas do
jogador.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Stack depth
Termo em inglês para “profundidade da pilha”. Indica
o stack médio de fichas entre os jogadores
envolvidos na ação.
Stack efetivo
Menor stack envolvido na ação.
Exemplo: você tem 60 blinds e seu oponente
tem 25. O stack efetivo é de 25 blinds.
Stack size
Tamanho do Stack de um jogador.
Stackear
Palavra em inglês para “empilhar”. No Brasil é usada
para indicar quando um jogador ganhou ou perdeu
muitas fichas de outro.
Exemplo: “eu estava gigante na mesa final mas
trombei com AA e fui stackeado”.

Standard
Palavra em inglês para “padrão”. Cenário ou jogada,
dentro do esperado.
Exemplo: “a mão que eu caí ontem foi bem
standard, eu fiz flush no turn, mandei três barris
mas o cara tinha full house”.
Stats
Palavra em inglês para “estatísticas”. No poker
usamos para avaliar as frequências de algumas
jogadas através de softwares de apoio ou HUD.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Exemplo: “quando vejo que a stat de 3bet do
oponente está maior que 15%, já sei que ele é
agressivo.”
Steal
Palavra em inglês para “roubo”. Nome do open raise
nas posições finais (hijack, cutoff ou button). Aposta
com objetivo de coletar o pote com o valor do small
e big blind.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Straddle
Termo em inglês para “atitude indecisa”. É uma
jogada do cash game, onde o jogador no UTG
compra o lugar do big blind, antes mesmo de ver
suas cartas e dos blinds serem coletados. O straddle
tem o valor de duas vezes o big blind e o jogador
passa a ser o último a agir no pré-flop.
Straight
Palavra em inglês para “direto”. É a sequência de
cinco cartas. É a 5ª mão mais forte dentre as dez
possíveis no Texas Hold’em. Ele é mais forte que
trinca e mais fraco que flush.
Straight draw
Palavra em inglês para “pedida para sequência”.
Quando você precisa de algumas cartas para formar
uma sequência.
Exemplo: você segura J8 e bate o flop 9-7-4.
Você precisa de um T no turn ou river para
completar uma sequência.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Straight flush
Combinação de cinco cartas sequenciadas do
mesmo naipe. É a 2ª mão mais forte dentre as dez
possíveis no Texas Hold’em. Ele é mais forte que a
quadra e está abaixo do royal straight flush.
Streets
Palavra em inglês para “ruas”. São as rodadas de
apostas no poker: pré-flop, flop, turn e river.
Stud
Abreviação de Seven Card Stud. Modalidade de
poker onde os jogadores recebem 7 cartas no total,
onde 3 cartas estão viradas para baixo e 4 para cima
e ganha quem tiver a melhor combinação de 5 cartas
do mesmo ranking de mãos do Texas Hold’em.
Suckout
Termo em inglês para “chupar”. Similar à bad beat,
indica um cenário onde uma mão muito forte é
superada por outra mais fraca.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Suited
Palavra em inglês para “adequado”. É uma gíria para
naipe.
Suited connector
Mãos naipadas e sequenciadas.
Exemplos: QJs, JTs, T9s, 98s, 76s, 65s, 54s,
43s.
Sunday Million
Torneio semanal no Pokerstars, acontece no
domingo e tem uma premiação garantida de, pelo
menos, U$ 1 milhão.
Swing
Palavra em inglês para “oscilação”. Um período de
resultados constantes, sejam eles positivos ou
negativos.
Variação: swingar é uma palavra abrasileirada que
significa “oscilar”.

Exemplo: Na reta final do torneio, fiquei
swingando meu stack até chegar na mesa final.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
t
Table selection
Palavra em inglês para seleção de mesas. Definir em
quais mesas você vai entrar durante o grind.
Exemplo: “eu tenho uma table selection muito
conservadora e jogo apenas quatro telas de sit
and go low mesmo com muita banca”.
TAG ou Tight Agressive
Termo em inglês para “agressivo apertado”. Indica
um perfil de jogador que escolhe jogar com um
leque de mãos composto pelo topo do baralho e faz
apostas de forma agressiva.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Exemplo: “aquele jogador TAG só tribeta mãos
mais fortes que JJ, cuidado com ele!”
Take it down
Termo em inglês para “detenha-o”. Quando o jogador
tem uma grande probabilidade de ganhar o pote se
decidir apostar contra os oponentes.
Tell
Palavra em inglês para “falar”. No poker indica
qualquer ação, comportamento ou mania específica
do jogador que indica, sem perceber, a força de sua
mão.
Exemplo: “meu amigo Thiago tem uma tell de
apostar muito rápido com seus blefes e demorar
para apostar com valor, ele sempre faz isso”.
Teoria
Vem do GTO - Game Theory Optimal ou Teoria do
Jogo Otimizado. Estuda o jogo de uma forma

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
equilibrada onde nenhum oponente tem vantagem
técnica sobre o outro e jogam de uma maneira
inexplorável. Os resultados de soluções em solvers,
sem nodelockes, podem ser considerados a teoria.
Thin value bet
Palavra em inglês para “aposta de valor fino”. É uma
aposta de valor com mão relativamente marginal,
que tem expectativa de ganhos próxima de 50% das
vezes em que recebe call do oponente.
Tight
Palavra em inglês para “apertado”. Indica um perfil
de jogador que joga com um leque de mãos
composto pelo topo do baralho no pré-flop e
contínua no pós-flop apenas com combos de muito
valor.
Exemplo: “aquele jogador é muito tight, só
aposta quando tem mão mais forte que top pair”.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Tilt
Palavra em inglês para “inclinar”. Gíria brasileira para
“ficar maluco”. Quando um jogador toma decisões
ruins após resultados negativos na mesa.
Exemplo: “depois de perder para uma bad beat,
aquele jogador tiltou e apostou all-in no escuro
três vezes seguidas”.
Top pair
Termo em inglês para “par superior”. É o par formado
com a carta mais alta na mesa. 
Atenção: não confunda top pair com overpair, que é
um par maior que as cartas no board.

Exemplo: você segura A9 no flop 9-7-3, então
tem o top pair. Mas se o oponente segura JJ, ele
tem um overpair.
Trap
Palavra em inglês para “armadilha”: Quando um

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
jogador faz jogadas passivas para esconder a força
da sua mão.
Exemplo: “aquele fish pensa que me engana
com limp do UTG, todo mundo sabe que ele faz
trap com AA”.
Trash
Palavra em inglês para “lixo”. As piores mãos no pré-
flop ou sem valor de showdown no pós-flop.
Trips
É uma trinca formada com duas cartas no board e
outra carta na mão do jogador.
Tournament Life
Termo em inglês para “vida no torneio”. Se refere à
sua permanência em torneios.
Exemplo: “eu evito me envolver em situações
marginais para preservar meu tournament life.”

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Third Barrel
Termo em inglês para “terceiro barril”. Ato de apostar
nas três rodadas de apostas do pós-flop: flop, turn e
river.
Exemplo: “meu amigo só vai para third barrel
quando tem valor no flop. Se ele acertar alguma
coisa no flop, vai mandar três barris”.
Turn
Palavra em inglês para “a volta”. Quarta carta
comunitária apresentada. Rodada de apostas depois
do flop.
Two pair
Termo em inglês para “dois pares”.  A terceira mão
mais fraca do Texas Hold’em.

u
Upswing
Palavra em inglês para “ascensão” ou “subida”. No
poker, refere-se a uma sequência consecutiva de
resultados lucrativos.
UTG
Sigla em inglês para Under the Gun ou “debaixo da
arma”. A primeira posição depois do big blind, numa
mesa completa com nove jogadores. Recebe esse
nome porque indica a pressão de ser o primeiro a
agir no pré-flop.
Under
Palavra em inglês para “embaixo”. Prefixo utilizado
para indicar algo menor.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
Underpair
Termo em inglês para “par abaixo de”. Quando você
segura um par menor que as cartas no board.
Exemplo: você segura 44 no flop T-7-5.
Underdog
Gíria em inglês para “azarão”. Indica um jogador com
uma mão fraca demais e poucas chances de ganhar
o pote.

v
Valor
Refere-se à força da mão.
Exemplo: um overbet no river representa muito
valor.
Valor de showdown ou Showdown value
Quando uma mão não acertou nada no board, mas
tem chances de superar a mão do oponente no
showdown. Exemplo: mãos com A-high.
Variância
Sequência de resultados positivos ou negativos,
dentro da normalidade. No poker, pode se referir aos

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
resultados financeiros após uma grande amostra de
torneios ou à resultados específicos de mãos em um
único torneio.
Exemplo: a variância do poker é muito alta para
você avaliar seu jogo depois de apenas 200
torneios. acesse o site Prime Dope para
entender melhor esse assunto.
Vilão
Seu oponente, adversário numa mão de poker.
VPIP
Sigla em inglês para “Voluntary Put Money in Pot” ou
“Colocar dinheiro voluntariamente no pote''. É uma
estatística que indica o percentual de vezes que o
jogador investiu dinheiro, voluntariamente, para
disputar um pote, seja pagando ou aumentando uma
aposta. Não contabiliza as apostas obrigatórias no
small e big blind.

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
w
Walk
Termo em inglês para “caminhada”. Quando todos na
mesa foldam e o big blind coleta o pote, sem
precisar jogar.
WCOOP
Sigla para World Championship Of Online Poker. O
Campeonato Mundial de Poker Online é uma série
anual de torneios online realizada no site Pokerstars,
com torneios de diferentes buy-Ins com premiações
garantidas maiores que as ofertadas nos torneios
diários.
Wide
Palavra em inglês para “amplo”. No poker refere-se a

chunks.source: Reg-Life_Dicionario-do-Poker.pdf
chunks.text:
um leque de mãos ou jogadas amplas.
Exemplo: eu prefiro cbetar no flop contra o big
blind porque sei que ele tem um range wide.
Winrate
Termo em inglês para “taxa de ganhos”. Estatística
que mede a sua lucratividade, seus ganhos em
determinado período de tempo ou número de jogos.
Exemplo: minha winrate no river aumentou
depois que eu passei a estudar conteúdo de
cash game.
Wired pair
Termo em inglês para “par com fio”. Quando você
recebe um par pronto no pré-flop. Diz-se que uma
carta puxou a outra, por isso é chamado de “par com
fio”.

WSOP
Sigla em inglês para World Series of Poker. Torneio
conhecido como o campeonato mundial de poker,
acontece anualmente em Las Vegas e os campeões
recebem braceletes dourados como troféu. A partir
de 2020, passou a ter sua versão online no site
GGPoker.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: Alexander Fitzgerald is a professional poker player who has been in the industry for over a decade. After running away from home during high school, Alex worked as a commercial fisherman and security guard, until he found success playing Texas Hold’em. While describing himself as having average intelligence, Alex has been able to accrue more than $3,500,000 in tournament earnings around the world. This includes final-tabling EPT (European Poker Tour) and multiple WCOOP (World Championship of Online Poker) events, along with practically every regular tournament online. In addition to his extraordinary success as a player, Alex also runs a poker consultancy which serves more than 1,000 professional poker players in 60 countries. Constantly at work, Alex has published hundreds of training videos, articles, and webinars. He is regarded by many as the most important tournament coach in the wo

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
Exploitative Play in Live Poker: How to Manipulate your Opponents into Making Mistakes

This Game is Not That Difficult

This game is not that difficult. Poker coaches just keep making it difficult for you. Did you ever play in a passive home game? Did you ever play in a poker game in 2004? Remember how everybody limped? Then one smart ass showed up. He’d visited a poker strategy site. He’d read a poker book. And he started raising. No one knew what to do, so they called him. Sometimes they beat him. More often than not, they didn’t.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
Eventually, everyone saw Gus Hansen raise anything on TV, and apparently always win. They wanted to be that guy too. So, slowly, over the years, they began opening anything. That’s as far as the game has gotten. If they are raising everything, you should be three-betting everything. It’s like there are two big blinds now. The actual big blind and the obligatory raise most players make with 30% of their hands from late position. You would raise constantly if there were two big blinds, even if the second one only appeared with an announcement from the dealer stating, “top 30% of hands has been declared; your action, sir.” You would re-raise with 10-9o, Q-8s. All manner of hands you do not “three-bet” now.

Why Do You Care What They Think?

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
I consulted for gaming companies for years. I’ve seen their books. Anywhere between 85 to 95 percent of players lose money at poker. The number is usually closer to 95 percent. This number only increases in live casino poker, as the rake increases. This means one thing: you are not playing well until everyone is making fun of you. If everybody sees your game and approves of it, that means you have gained the approval of losers. In order to win, you must ruffle their feathers and play in a style contrary to their unprofitable strategies. Does anyone ever notice you at the poker table? Or have you gained the acceptance of losers?

I Know You Care What They Think

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
How many times have you said to yourself, “Wow, I can’t believe he opened with that”? When was the last time you did something about it? When was the last time you waged war against a table of weak openers? Or were you afraid of being the table’s resident three-betting “asshole”?

If you do not take risks for your opinion, you are nothing. –

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: In The Myth of Poker Talent, I discussed how to study. In Exploitative Play in Live Poker, I will discuss the conclusions of my studies. Equity calculators and data collection of live events will be condensed into easily understood macro lessons. Live poker is uniquely suited to my work, because 99 percent of the time in live play you know very little about your opponent. In those situations, you must make a judgment call on what the masses will do with an Ace-high or three of a kind. I will present my conclusions in a simple format. Most poker coaches refuse to do this because if you present an idea simply then you can be held accountable. If an idea is complex, the teacher can always say, “You didn’t understand me. You did it wrong. Your losses are your fault.” If an idea is simple to implement and it does not work, then the student knows exactly who to blame.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
Why Some Feel MOPT was Worth $5,000 a Copy

The Myth of Poker Talent was not the book I wanted to write. It was the book I knew had to be written. For those of you who did not read the book, my simple conjecture within the pages was, “Poker is not a game of reading souls. It is a game of counting combinations. There is a way to use software to do this and through rigorous analysis and study you can synthesize the hand-reading skills that some top-level pros have.” I wrote the book partially out of frustration from my lessons.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: After Black Friday saw me losing $100,000+ overnight, I said to myself, “I can never rely on this game again.” I love poker with all my heart, but I knew we had to become just friends. I enjoyed my time as a full-time professional poker player greatly. While I was never a major league talent, I was able to rack up WCOOP and SCOOP wins while also final tabling WPTs and EPTs. I had a lot of fun playing every day. But as you get older, you start wanting to diversify. As you gather more dependents, a constant paycheck starts looking more appetizing. I started my coaching consultancy in 2011. I called it Assassinato Coaching. I had no website. I had no secretary. I didn’t even know how to use calendaring software. But I opened my digital doors anyway.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: Coaching was initially a hobby that paid for my rent, cable, electricity, and groceries. I always considered coaching five times as difficult as playing poker, and more exhausting. I have not changed my opinion. However, the more I coached, the more I found the work engrossing. Delving deeply into the problems of poker was challenging, invigorating, and illuminating. I took pride in seeing my students win. Over eight years, I got better at my craft. My students, thankfully, started racking up the wins. I took classes on how to become a better coach. My lessons soon delivered a punch. They always had actionable advice. However, at the end of the lesson I’d always say to my pupils, “okay, remember that Cardrunners EV/Flopzilla software we used? I want you to try and use it a few times before we meet next time. Just get the feel for it.” 98% of my students would not do so. This frustrated m

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: e greatly, because I knew they were intelligent people. Part of my difficulty was I had so few hours with them. I would estimate that I invested 25,000+ hours into No Limit Hold’em before I felt truly comfortable with it. My wealthiest students purchased 20-hour packages. It was still just a drop in the ocean.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: My second difficulty was if someone saw me using poker software for a couple hours it was still very little exposure. They got the gist of what I was doing, but not the full scope. Due to the admitted gaps in knowledge, they didn’t want to throw themselves into the task of deep poker study. It felt like a fruitless endeavor to them. The short time they would spend seeing me use the software wasn’t enough. They would run into snags during the first few hours of making their own ranges and feel immensely frustrated, as if they were wasting their time. I had blown a gasket the first time I used Cardrunners EV, because software and I have never got along. A few hours later, I realized that I had simply made a couple of innocent mistakes with the program. A hundred hours later, I discovered five or so other small mistakes anyone could make. I thought, “I’ll document all of these issues and tu

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
rn it into a guide. Then, boom. Whenever my students are struggling, I will send them this book. They’ll get to work on their game effectively, and I’ll be set.”

D&B Poker picked up the book about poker study using software. I set to writing it. I never felt that comfortable with poker software. I only learned how to use the programs because it was a necessity. I was worried I got something wrong in the hundreds of pages of analysis. That’s why the response to the book was so surprising to me. “This is the best poker book I have ever read; and it’s not even close,” one reviewer at a poker site commented. “I wish this book could be unpublished or sold for $5,000 a copy,” lamented another poker player. “The revolution is complete!” I joked to myself. I thought this guide would get all my players up to speed. Except it didn’t.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: There is a ton of material in The Myth of Poker Talent. For example, I proved that on certain boards you can close your eyes, triple barrel any turn and river card and you’ll still make a profit. Of course, there were some parameters. Your opponent had to be calling wide from the big blind and capping their range on the flop. They had to be calling with only second pair or better on the river. But hey, I thought that was pretty damn impressive! Look at how often we should be triple barreling! Except no one cared. I thought that section of the book would really cause a discussion among my students. Instead, none of them seemed to notice.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: When I flipped through that part of the book, I saw why. There are pages upon pages of minutiae before the final conjecture is made. Anyone who was skimming through would probably skip the section. This dispirited me. I loved that the final product of The Myth of Poker Talent reached so many people and helped their games, but I wanted it to reach more of them. But, as one hyper-intelligent person put it, “Just because something is based in emotion doesn’t mean it’s any less real.” If people don’t want to perform long, intricate calculations to come up with their poker plays, then you have to find another way to help them.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: It was unfair of me to expect everyone to share my enthusiasm for studying poker. Most people want to play poker. Not study it. 90% of my clients are working in a real job. Many have kids. It’s hard for them to find time to even play poker, much less study it. They don’t have 60 hours a week like I do.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
So, for this book, let’s make a new agreement. Your job is to learn how to become better at something you love. You are doing this for your own satisfaction and enjoyment. My job is to give you the quickest path to success. My job is not to explain to you every single thing I think about poker. I wouldn’t wish that on my worst enemy. You can refer to the first book if you ever want to check one of my plays. But, for this book, I’m going to try to be the best teacher I can be, as opposed to the most intense. The best teacher is not the most intelligent teacher. It is the teacher who gets the most information to his students. There is a big difference between the two.

This was lost on me for many years. I couldn’t figure out why I got so much information out of Matthew Janda, a guy who admits he doesn’t play much, but I wasn’t getting much of anything out of some of the great players.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: It was because the best poker players don’t always make the best coaches. Sometimes the information they convey is entertaining but doesn’t work for normal poker games. A good golf coach is a better example of how to teach more effectively. They might have been a pro at one time. They might still go out for the U.S. Open and compete. They could no doubt fill up multiple books with what they think about golf. However, when this coach is teaching you, they focus on one thing at a time. “Turn your hips this way on the drive”, “hold your hands like this when you putt”, and so on. And they make you do it again and again in front of them. Then, it’s up to you to do it in your free time.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
However, with just this system, you will have an edge the next time you play. You will know what the professional told you to do. You will focus on it. You will improve. If you improve on enough facets of your game you might become a scratch golfer. At that point you can think about the PGA tour. But you’ll only get there by focusing on one thing at a time. All the small technical changes eventually turn into one large one. You’re still going to have to play a ton of golf, but with this methodology you have a fighting chance of making it.

“I really wish you never wrote that damn book,” one of my friends told me over the phone.

“Yeah, well, you know what they say: your book is your business card now,” I replied.

“You know who your game really helps in [Californian cardroom]?”

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
“40-year-old guys. 50-year-old guys. I can’t continuation-bet into a J-5-4 board anymore without getting check-raised.”

I heard a version of this conversation constantly after The Myth of Poker Talent was published. One student even told me, “I never check-raise a board anymore. Everybody has read that chapter in your book.” I wanted to know why that powerful play caught on with my students, but others didn’t. When I turned to that part of the book, I could see why. The tone of that part of the book is conversational. The math is simplified into a few numbers. It’s like a golf coach breaking down his expertise into concise English.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
After the release of The Myth of Poker Talent I received a new wave of students. It’s true what they say; your book now is your true business card. To my surprise, most of the students were not professional poker players. My clients now were working professionals and blue-collar workers. Doctors, lawyers, priests, mechanics, nurses, business consultants, electricians, DJs, bartenders, IT specialists, truck drivers, and politicians all came through my digital doors. They all seemed to say the same thing to me. “Is there any way you can simplify everything you wrote in the book for me? The few sections I did understand really helped me make more money.” This book is my attempt to answer them.

How has Tournament Poker Changed in Two Years?

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: I do not believe tournament poker is getting tougher. No one folds their big blind or open raise any more. They prefer to flat three-bets out of position. They prefer to call from the big blind, seemingly regardless of the bet sizing. This is a very good thing. Now, to be fair to the field, they weren’t wrong to begin flatting more from the big blind and flatting three-bets out of position.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: If you open raise to 2.5 big blinds and then fold to a re-raise, you are losing 250 big blinds per 100 hands played. That is a lot of money. That’s how much money J-J makes over 100 hands. That’s how much money you’re giving up. If you flat out of position and take a flop you’re not losing 250 big blinds per 100 hands played in this fashion. You can save some money by fighting with the guy. However, 90% of players are still losing money when they flat out of position. And many of the remaining 10% are just running well.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: A similar thing happens when you’re in the big blind. If you just muck your big blind then you’re losing 100 big blinds for every 100 hands you play (duh). But if you fight with the raiser just a bit, you can save some of those big blinds. It doesn’t take much to improve. Now, what I just said above is true, but it was much more true when those strategies first became popular.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: Why? Back in 2012, when these strategies caught on, open raises were 2 big blinds. Your pot odds to call were incredible. If you three-bet large or raised preflop to large amounts then people still called you out of position. This can create some stunning losses for the out-of-position flatter. I constantly open to four times the big blind. Nobody wants to three-bet the large open, but they will call from the big blind. The average person is not folding 6-4s from the lojack now, or even J-9s UTG. This makes hands like Q-Jo a value three-bet. That hand used to not even be a two-bet. And, if people keep calling you out of position, that’s great for you. I don’t care how bad you are at poker. If your opponents are willing to play big pots with you out of position with mediocre hands, then you’re going to make money.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: All my strategies were created based on population tendencies in both live cash games and tournaments. I consulted hundreds of people around the world who were keeping data on live games to construct these strategies. This book is primarily designed for live poker tournaments and cash games played in North America. They also function very well in the Caribbean and Latin America, since many players within those user bases are North American or are heavily influenced by North Americans. These strategies work well in Western Europe and all of the English-speaking world. These strategies should be of great use to you in poker tournaments with buy-ins up to $3,500. They are also effective in cash games up to $2/$5.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: However, Las Vegas is a different matter due to the large concentration of poker players. In that market, I would limit buy-ins to $2,000 or less in tournaments. I also wouldn’t apply these methods in any cash game above $1/$2. I applied this playbook against a number of Russian players during a deep run in a PCA $5,000 event. I also applied it during my WPT final table run in Prague, which saw me playing a field largely composed of Eastern Europeans. I found players from this region of the world to be the most aware of what I was doing. Many players still fell for my traps but several others were wise to my plays. This awareness was far less pronounced in events with buy-ins of $1,000 or less. The adjustments I made were dropping my riskier bluffs. I three-bet less, because they were opening fewer hands. I check-raised less from the big blind for the same reason. In my opinion, these st

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
rategies will work in 99% of No Limit Hold’em games on Earth, cash and tournament, especially once you know what to look for. But if you have a choice in the matter, head for North America and play tournaments. That is where the leaks are most pronounced.

Now that we’re well acquainted, let’s start discussing how to play cards. First off, you need to understand that most of what you know about poker is bull. This is not a sport. Every time you pout about a bad beat you sound like an idiot. This is a hustling game. Pure and simple. Granted, it is a domesticated hustling game. It is a game where gentlemen can mutually agree to play at hustling each other for a few hours, and then retire to their family home where they are honest members of society.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
That said, poker began as a hustling game and, due to this, it still rewards players who think of it as a hustle. Employees on the Titanic were told to keep a lookout for cardsharps who were introducing the game of poker to wealthier patrons. That was in 1912. The game was initially played with 20 cards. I am fully convinced that they switched to a 52-card game on the Mississippi river because it was more likely to confuse riverboat occupants. The odds of this game are meant to be confusing. Don’t let them confuse you. If you need a 100,000+ word primer on what the odds are in damn near every spot, I direct you to my first book.

I will discuss specific concepts in the forthcoming chapters, but you need to remember this.

When you play cards with someone less skilled than you, then you are effectively a pool hustler.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
Pool hustlers don’t always win. One of the great joys of hanging out in a pool hall is to see a pool hustler get hustled. It is a sanguine art that is largely lost. But it lives in this game. Poker has a built-in feature that allows you to “throw the game.” Someone who doesn’t understand the odds will see you not rake in a pot, and will assume you are a loser. They will not understand that you are just letting a game go before you hike up the stakes.

Now, remember this, because truer words have never been spoken.

Pool hustlers do not sink every trick shot.

Even if you hit that corner pocket nine times out of ten there is always that potential miss. I don’t care who you are. You can up the stakes with a “mark” and miss your shot. And I hate to tell you this, but you’re never 90% to win in poker. 80% is the most you’ll ever get. Many times, you ride right around 60%.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: Poker is a fun game, but it’s just a game. It is a game of some information, not total information. It is a game of some luck, but not total luck. It is a game of some skill, but not total skill. It is a game of hustling that doesn’t always reward the hustler. It is a card game that steals from the artists to give to the scientists who then get robbed by the hustlers, before they give it back to the artists again. It is hilariously broken. You will die 500 years before your luck catches up to you. No game contains your redemption, so look not for it here. It is beautiful because it is so meaningless. Chess is knowledge. Poker is wisdom. Anyone can win on any day. And if you want to win in this game, you’re going to love that fact even when you hate it.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
You ready to begin? Great. Me too. I am happy to be on this journey with you. However, before I teach you how to actually play cards, I need you to understand your enemy first. This next chapter will change all of the hands we play for the rest of our lives.

Exploitative Play in Live Poker: How to Manipulate your Opponents into Making Mistakes

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
If you were to Google “stock market trends analysis” how many articles would you find? The correct answer is 49,000,000. Now, if you were to Google “poker field trend analysis” what would you find? 390,000 results. Not a bad haul! Except the first result, or what Google believes is the best match for what you’re looking for based on everything that’s on the internet, is a prediction article on who is going to win the 2015 WSOP Main Event. The second-best result is a fairly well-written paper on how someone one day could possibly do population analysis.

♦ What is considered a normal batting average in Major League Baseball?

♦ What is an average NBA player’s PPG? (Points Per Game)

♦ What is an average NHL player’s PPG?

♦ What is an average Premier League player’s PPG?

♦ What is the average three-betting percentage of a player in your favorite poker room?

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
Your three enemies in No Limit Hold’em are yourself, the field, and time. Most people actually know how to play winning No Limit Hold’em. They just don’t have the willpower to execute.

One of my students has a wife. She is my hero. She plays J-J, Q-Q, K-K, and A-A. She also plays A-K and A-Q when she’s feeling a little naughty. If you three-bet her, she’s likely to fold A-Q, A-K, and J-J. If she four-bets you, it’s almost always aces. She crushes. She always crushes. Men can’t stand to see women winning, especially one employing such a damn basic strategy. They think it says something about them, that such a simplistic ploy could best them. They seek to punish the woman for even being in their games. And that’s when they run into her aces.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: When I started playing poker, I didn’t have a pot to piss in. I played 20 hands, almost all premiums. If you three-bet me or raised my flop continuation-bet, I was very likely to fold. I made money hand over fist with this strategy. The reason 95% of people lose at No Limit Hold’em is they play too many hands, and they play them poorly. They play passively, out of position, and in large pots they have no business being in. They play mediocre holdings without a plan, and then moan when their garbage pair gets overtaken by the superior starting hand which always had greater potential.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
For these reasons, your greatest enemy at the poker table is always yourself. “In the long run, we are all dead,” is how the famous British economist John Maynard Keynes put it. You need millions of hands to begin developing yourself as a professional poker player. You need millions more to become the best player you can be.

In live poker, we’re lucky to get more than 100 hands played in a day. If you are looking for redemption or for success in life, you’d do better than to look for it in the arms of a game of chance. You will never get your due in poker, good or bad. Finally, let’s discuss the enemy we can do the most about. His name is “the field”.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
When the Philadelphia Eagles were preparing for Super Bowl LII they had quite a daunting task ahead of them. Their competition, the New England Patriots, were heavily favored for a good reason. They are considered by many to be the greatest dynasty in the history of the sport. Their quarterback, Tom Brady, is widely referred to as “the GOAT”, even by his detractors. GOAT here, of course, stands for Greatest Of All Time.

The Philadelphia Eagles, on the other hand, had been established during World War II, and had never yet won a championship. Tom Brady, for reference, has five championship wins. Philadelphia’s quarterback wasn’t even a starter. Nick Foles, a journeyman backup, had shown early promise in the league and then washed out. He was only playing for Philadelphia because their normal starter had been injured.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
If you were managing and coaching the Philadelphia Eagles for this game, where would you start? Would you look at Nick Foles for new potential? Would you try to get something out of your team that no scout had discovered in all the years the players had been playing? Or would you be looking at the Patriots for minor weaknesses you could exploit?

What if I told you the field you were facing was not the New England Patriots? What if I told you that they weren’t even a high school football team? What if I told you that it’s your own lack of preparation that sinks you at the table and it has nothing to do with the opposition?

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
Look, I can prove it to you. Pull out your scouting report on the field. Come on. Let’s see it. You tell everyone you’re a serious player. Everyone in your social circle knows you as “the poker guy”. So, I assume you have kept notes on your opponents, like every single sportsman does on his opponents. At the very least, I know you have some broad generalizations on the field that generally hold true. So come on. Pull it out of your desk or Evernote files. Let’s take a look. If you have nothing to show me right now, I will ask why that is.

In which confrontational sport do people not analyze their opposition? Chess masters study their opponents’ games. Even high school football coaches, who are getting paid nothing, examine their opposition.

I’m going to ask you the following kind of questions again and again.

♦ How often does the average poker player check-raise on the flop?

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
♦ How often does the average player raise you on the river?

♦ When someone three-bets you preflop without moving all-in, what hands do they generally have?

♦ How do you generally respond to these players?

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: If you have not thought about what the common poker player thinks, then you have a serious problem. In 99% of poker games, you do not play against the same opposition. In tournament poker, you generally get to play 40 to 100 hands with an opponent before they move on, never to be seen again. In cash games, especially lower stakes ones, there’s a rotating cast of tourists who come in and out. Of course, specialized reads are preferable, but most of the time you will not have this luxury. You will need to know how the average human behaves when they are faced with financial decisions, and there are ways to cultivate this information. Notecaddy has terrific data mapping features. Hold’em Manager and Poker Tracker allow you to cull through databases to see how people react to different betting opportunities online. You can also do what I did, which is the most boring option of them all – wat

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text:
ch more poker than anyone on Earth.

That is not hyperbole. I would wager most of my net worth on the fact no one has watched as much tournament poker as I have. My students play live and online. They bring me their hand histories, live streams, and recorded confrontations. For four to six hours every day, five days a week, for the last eight years, I have watched all of this poker. During much of this time I was still playing poker eight hours a day. While this time investment has me questioning what I did with my twenties, it does have some advantages.

chunks.source: Alexander Fitzgerald - Excelling at Live Poker-D&b Publishing (2018)
chunks.text: For one, I can run through my memory and think if any particular country does not adhere to a particular data point. I can see which statistical breakdowns really pass my experiential recall. This allows me to have a second check on all of my findings that wouldn’t be available to data scientists working on the problem of No Limit Hold’em. I also have the benefit of testing. I have developed my own playbooks based on what the data says the field is doing. I have released these playbooks to my students, and they have applied the methods across tens of millions of hands, if not hundreds of millions. They have played tens of thousands of tournaments with these ideas. Largely, they have reported success.

chunks.text: Why Play Poker? The allure of poker lies in its fascinating mix of skill, strategy, chance, and psychology. With its roots extending over a millennium, poker has evolved into a global pastime that transcends boundaries of age, culture, and socio-economic status. So, why should one play poker? This section explores the myriad reasons that make this card game a compelling pursuit for millions around the globe. Poker is often perceived as a competitive platform that pits mind against mind, offering an exciting arena to test one's strategic thinking, decision-making skills, and ability to handle pressure. This mental challenge is a significant draw for many players. The satisfaction of outsmarting opponents through skilled plays and successful bluffs makes poker much more than just a game of chance.

chunks.source: Derick Crawford - How to Play Poker for Beginners
chunks.text: Unlike many other card games where the outcome depends heavily on luck, poker rewards skill and strategy. While the luck of the draw does play a part, over the long run, a player's understanding of poker strategy, knowledge of odds, and reading of other players, heavily influences their success. This underscores poker's appeal as a game of skill. Another compelling reason to play poker is the psychological aspect. Poker is as much about playing the cards as it is about playing the people. The ability to read opponents, to detect patterns, weaknesses, and tells, adds a layer of intrigue that pushes poker beyond a simple card game. This psychological duel makes poker an engaging and rewarding pursuit.

chunks.source: Derick Crawford - How to Play Poker for Beginners
chunks.text: The social aspect of poker should not be underestimated. Whether it's a casual game with friends or a tournament with strangers, poker offers a communal experience that brings people together. The shared excitement, tension, and camaraderie fostered around a poker table create a unique social bonding experience that few other games can offer. The potential for financial gain, too, plays a role in poker's appeal. The prospect of winning money, sometimes large amounts, adds an element of thrill and aspiration. From local cash games to high-stakes tournaments, the promise of a financial reward adds a tantalizing edge to the poker experience.

chunks.source: Derick Crawford - How to Play Poker for Beginners
chunks.text: Finally, poker is a journey of continuous learning. With every hand you play, you gain insights about the game, your opponents, and even yourself. This journey of self-improvement and the satisfaction derived from refining your strategy, improving your skills, and overcoming challenges are incredibly fulfilling. In summary, people play poker for various reasons: the intellectual challenge, the competitive thrill, the social interaction, the potential financial rewards, and the ongoing journey of learning and self-improvement. Regardless of the motivation, poker offers an engaging and rewarding experience that captivates players worldwide.

chunks.text: Understanding the Popularity of Poker The universal appeal of poker, a game that deftly blends skill, strategy, chance, and psychology, is undeniably magnetic. It draws in a diverse range of enthusiasts worldwide, each drawn by different aspects of this multi-faceted game. This section delves into the various factors contributing to poker's popularity, painting a picture of why this age-old card game has managed to captivate so many. Firstly, poker's unique combination of skill and luck is a major allure. Unlike many games that are either skill-based like chess or dependent solely on luck like roulette, poker marries these two elements. The cards you're dealt are entirely up to chance, but how you play them, is a test of skill and strategy. This engaging blend of elements provides an exciting platform for mental gymnastics, making every round a fresh puzzle to solve.

chunks.source: Derick Crawford - How to Play Poker for Beginners
chunks.text: The competitive nature of poker also contributes significantly to its appeal. It's a battle of minds, where you compete against others, not just against the odds. This player-versus-player competition adds a thrilling dimension of human interaction, with each game being a strategic contest filled with bluffs, calculated risks, and tactical retreats. Poker is inherently social, which adds to its popularity. Whether it's a casual family game, a regular community meetup, or a global tournament, poker fosters a sense of community. The experience of sharing a table with others, the friendly banter, the shared anticipation of the next card, and the camaraderie, all make poker an enriching social activity.

chunks.source: Derick Crawford - How to Play Poker for Beginners
chunks.text: The potential for financial gain is another enticing aspect of poker. Stories of players turning small buy-ins into substantial winnings in high-stakes games and tournaments are part of poker's charm. This promise of financial success, combined with the glamour of poker scenes in movies and television, contributes to the game's widespread appeal. However, poker's appeal extends beyond the potential for monetary winnings. The game, for many, is an ongoing journey of learning and self-improvement. Each hand offers a new opportunity to learn, to adapt, and to hone your skills. This constant evolution, the satisfaction derived from a well-played hand, the thrill of a bluff gone right, and the continual quest for mastery are what truly make poker an enduring passion for many.

chunks.source: Derick Crawford - How to Play Poker for Beginners
chunks.text: In conclusion, poker's popularity can be attributed to its unique blend of skill and chance, its competitive nature, the social connections it fosters, the potential for financial reward, and the continuous journey of learning and improvement it offers. Whether for fun, profit, competition, or personal growth, poker holds an appeal that few other games can match.

chunks.source: Derick Crawford - How to Play Poker for Beginners
chunks.text: Overview of the Book This comprehensive guide to poker is designed to equip you with the knowledge and skills required to fully appreciate and engage in the game. Over the course of this book, we will delve into the various aspects of poker that make it such a captivating pursuit for millions around the world. In Chapter 2, "The History of Poker," we will delve into the origins of this compelling card game, tracing its evolution over centuries and across continents. We’ll examine how poker has grown and changed over the years, from a rudimentary card game to a globally recognized sport.

chunks.source: Derick Crawford - How to Play Poker for Beginners
chunks.text: Chapter 3, "Understanding Poker Basics," will provide a solid foundation for newcomers to the game. From understanding poker hand rankings to the mechanics of betting, this chapter is designed to demystify the game and equip you with the basic knowledge required to play. In Chapter 4, "Diving Deeper: Poker Variants," we will explore the many forms of poker that exist today, such as Texas Hold’em, Omaha, Seven-Card Stud, and more. Each variant comes with its own unique strategies and appeals, further enriching the game's complexity and intrigue. Chapter 5, "The Art of Strategy," delves into the importance of strategic thinking in poker. We'll discuss concepts such as position, pot odds, bluffing, and understanding player types, to equip you with the strategic tools to outmaneuver your opponents.

chunks.source: Derick Crawford - How to Play Poker for Beginners
chunks.text: In Chapter 6, "Reading Your Opponents: Poker Psychology," we will delve into the human element of poker. Understanding tells, managing emotions, and leveraging psychological insights to gain an edge over your opponents are some of the topics we'll explore. Chapter 7, "Poker Etiquette," addresses the social aspect of poker. Here, we'll outline the do's and don'ts at the poker table to ensure you are a respected player, whether you're engaging in a friendly home game or a high-stakes tournament. Chapter 8, "Bankroll Management," will teach you how to handle your poker finances responsibly, enabling you to enjoy the game in a sustainable and stress-free manner, irrespective of whether you play for fun or for a living.

chunks.source: Derick Crawford - How to Play Poker for Beginners
